messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Frank is a 74-year-old widower and former combat pilot who spent decades in the cockpit of fighter jets, accustomed to precision, control, and the absolute clarity of a mission. What shattered him was not enemy fire, but the slow, intimate violence of his second wife, Helen. Over the final three years of their marriage, her drinking would escalate from wine with dinner to a mean, unpredictable intoxication. In those states, she would corner him in the kitchen, slap him across the face, or dig her fingernails into his forearm until he bled—always when he was off-guard, always when he was trying to de-escalate. He never hit back. A pilot does not fire on his own wingman. He absorbed it, told himself it was the alcohol talking, and stayed quiet.

Now, three years after her death from liver failure, Frank lives alone in a tidy apartment near the airbase where he works part-time as a flight simulator instructor. The job keeps him busy, but the environment has become a minefield. The smell of rubbing alcohol from the cleaning crew’s supply closet hits him in the hallway every Tuesday morning, and his stomach clenches before he can name why. A student’s accidental hand on his shoulder during a debrief sends a jolt through his chest that takes minutes to settle. Worst of all is seeing a woman with Helen’s build—stocky, dark-haired, walking with that same forward-leaning stride—in the commissary. His throat tightens, his palms go slick, and he finds an excuse to leave.

In response to these triggers, Frank has built a set of rules he follows without question. He never allows himself to feel or express anger—not even when a student makes a dangerous error or a colleague cuts him off in the parking lot. He has come to believe that anger is a door he must never open, because once it swings wide, he might not be able to stop what comes through. He also avoids anything that reminds him of Helen: he threw out her clothes, donated the furniture from their shared bedroom, and stopped driving past the restaurant where they used to eat. And he avoids intimacy with a discipline that feels almost professional. When a friendly neighbor invites him for coffee, he declines. When his daughter calls to check in, he keeps the conversation under five minutes and ends it with a firm “I’m fine.” He has become convinced that closeness means vulnerability, and vulnerability is what got him hurt.

The problem is that these strategies do not work the way he hoped. The more he suppresses his anger, the more his body stays on high alert. At night, lying in bed, he cannot let his guard down. He sleeps in short, restless cycles, hyperaware of every creak in the hallway, every distant car door—because in his mind, danger does not announce itself. His hypervigilance has become a permanent state: scanning faces in the grocery store, watching doorways, listening for the tell-tale clink of a bottle. And when something reminds him of the abuse—a touch, a smell, a glimpse of a woman with Helen’s posture—his heart slams against his ribs, his breath goes shallow, and he feels the old surge of adrenaline that used to tell him to brace for impact.

These physical reactions, in turn, make him more sensitive to triggers. A single startle response in the simulator leaves him scanning the room for the rest of the shift. A sleepless night makes him jumpy and irritable the next day, which he interprets as a sign that he is losing control. So he tightens his rules. He avoids more. He stays home more often. He tells himself that if he can just manage his environment perfectly, he will be safe.

But the environment is not the problem. The problem is that his body remembers what his mind tries to bury. He came to therapy because his daughter, worried after a third canceled holiday visit, asked him directly: “Dad, what are you so afraid of?” He could not answer her out loud, but the question has stayed with him. What he is most afraid of is that the woman who hurt him is gone, and yet he is still living inside her reach—that he has become a man who cannot be touched, cannot be angry, cannot be close to anyone, and that this is not survival but a slow, quiet kind of dying. He does not know if he can unlearn the rules that kept him safe, but he knows he cannot keep living by them.
